summary: Proposes using OAuth 2.0 to get and validate short-lived tokens for STUN authentication. Because the tokens are ephemeral, access to a STUN server can still be controlled even if a token is stolen.

eli5.summary: Instead of giving everyone a permanent key, you hand out a ticket that stops working soon. Even if a ticket is stolen, it is not much use.

questions: how to use oauth with stun
what is the stun access-token attribute
how does turn third-party authorization work
what is the third-party-authorization stun attribute
subtitle: How STUN and TURN servers can accept short-lived OAuth 2.0 tokens instead of shared passwords.

tldr.problem: STUN's long-term username/password credentials are expected to stay secret, but in web applications such as WebRTC, where JavaScript makes the calls, that secrecy is typically not possible.
tldr.mechanism: A client gets an ephemeral, self-contained OAuth 2.0 token from an authorization server and puts it in a new ACCESS-TOKEN attribute. The STUN server decrypts it with a key it shares with the authorization server and uses the session key inside to check message integrity.
tldr.outcome: Access to a STUN or TURN server can still be controlled even if a token is compromised, because tokens are short-lived. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7635 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Long-Term Credentials
sections.content:
STUN (RFC 5389) controls access with 'long-term' username/password credentials that are part of the STUN protocol. Those credentials are expected to be kept secret. If they are discovered, the STUN server could be used by unauthorized users or applications.

In web applications like WebRTC, where JavaScript uses the browser for real-time audio and video calls, ensuring that secrecy is typically not possible. RFC 7635 proposes third-party authorization with OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) instead. A client obtains an ephemeral token from an authorization server, for example a WebRTC server, and presents that token to the STUN server in place of username/password credentials. The same approach can be used with TURN (RFC 5766).
sections.eli5: A password that every web page visitor can see is not much of a secret. A ticket that only works for a short while is safer to hand out.

sections.title: Solution Overview
sections.content:
A STUN client learns that it can use OAuth 2.0 with a server either through configuration or when it receives the new THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION attribute in an error response with error code 401 (Unauthorized).

The RFC uses the token type 'Assertion', also called a self-contained token, from RFC 6819. All the information needed to check the token is inside the token, so the STUN server does not need to talk to the authorization server to validate it, which reduces latency. The token is opaque to the client. The OAuth 2.0 grant type is 'Implicit', where the client is issued an access token directly, and the string stun is defined as the OAuth scope value.

How a client actually obtains a token is outside the scope of the RFC. Appendix B gives an example HTTP exchange.

For TURN, the resource owner (the WebRTC server) authorizes a TURN client to use a TURN server (the resource server). The TURN client sends an Allocate request without credentials, is told 401 with THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION, gets a token, and retries with ACCESS-TOKEN included.
sections.eli5: The server says 'I need a ticket.' You go to the ticket office, get one, and show it at the door. The door guard can check the ticket without phoning the office.

sections.title: Keys Between the Servers
sections.content:
The STUN server does not authenticate the client directly. It checks whether the client knows the session key (mac_key) tied to a specific access token. The authorization server shares a long-term secret K with the STUN server. When a client asks for a token, the authorization server creates a fresh session key and places it in the token, encrypted with K.

Symmetric cryptography MUST be used, because asymmetric cryptography gives large encrypted tokens that may not fit in a single STUN message. The two servers MUST establish K over an authenticated secure channel, but how is out of scope.

Two examples are given. In the HTTP option, the STUN server makes an HTTP GET to the authorization server at a .well-known/stun-key path over HTTPS, with TLS client certificates for mutual authentication, and gets back a JSON object with the key (k), an expiry (exp), a kid and the algorithm (enc). Implementations MUST support A256GCM. The other option is manual provisioning of the key, algorithm and kid, which needs a configuration change to rotate, so implementations SHOULD support the REST method.
sections.eli5: The ticket office and the door guard share a secret code ahead of time. The ticket is locked with that code, so only the guard can open it.

sections.title: The New Attributes and the Token
sections.content:
After a 401 response, the client retries with the token and kid in the ACCESS-TOKEN and USERNAME attributes. The last attribute is MESSAGE-INTEGRITY, an HMAC computed as in RFC 5389 but using mac_key as the key, with no MD5 hash of credentials.

THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION carries the STUN server name. It is comprehension-optional. A client that understands it MUST give third-party authorization precedence over first-party authentication. A client that cannot do third-party authorization defaults to first-party authentication.

ACCESS-TOKEN is comprehension-required and holds the token, which must fit within the maximum STUN message size (STUN messages over IPv4 would need to be less than 548 bytes if the path MTU is unknown). The client MUST NOT examine the token. The token holds a nonce length and nonce, then an encrypted block with the key length, the mac_key, a 64-bit timestamp and a 32-bit lifetime in seconds. The key length of 160 bits MUST be supported. The associated data for encryption MUST be the STUN server name, so a token cannot be used on another STUN server in the same administrative domain that shares the same key. The whole token is base64 encoded.
sections.eli5: The ticket has a sealed envelope inside with a secret code, a time stamp and an expiry time. You are not allowed to open the envelope, only the guard can.

sections.title: Server, Client and TURN Behavior
sections.content:
On a request with ACCESS-TOKEN, the STUN server picks the key material using the kid from USERNAME and decrypts the token. If authenticated decryption fails, the request is rejected with 401. The server then retrieves mac_key and checks for replay: the token is accepted only if lifetime + Delta > abs(RDnew - TS), where the recommended Delta is 5 seconds. Finally it verifies MESSAGE-INTEGRITY with mac_key. Any failure gives a 401. Every response MUST include MESSAGE-INTEGRITY computed with mac_key. If a server gets ACCESS-TOKEN without having sent THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION, it answers 420 (Unknown Attribute).

The client discards any response whose MESSAGE-INTEGRITY is missing or wrong. When the token expires, it MUST get a new one.

For TURN, one token can be reused for multiple Allocate requests to the same server, and the client includes ACCESS-TOKEN only in Allocate and Refresh requests. The lifetime the TURN server returns MUST be less than or equal to the token lifetime. The client uses the new token to refresh existing allocations, so it keeps only one token per TURN server.
sections.eli5: The guard opens the envelope, checks the ticket is fresh and then talks to you using the secret code so you both know nobody else is pretending. When the ticket runs out, you fetch a new one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
When OAuth 2.0 is used, the client's exchange with the authorization server requires TLS with a ciphersuite offering confidentiality, following RFC 7525. The session key MUST NOT be sent in clear, since that would destroy the security benefit.

Replay of a message with ACCESS-TOKEN can be mitigated by frequent changes of the nonce value. A client may know some but not all of the encrypted token fields, so the token could face known-plaintext attacks, but AES is secure against this attack.

An attacker could remove the THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION attribute from the error message to force the client back to first-party authentication. This can be mitigated by running STUN over TLS or DTLS.
sections.eli5: Never shout the secret code across the playground. And a sneaky person might hide the sign saying 'bring a ticket', so it is safer to talk over a private line.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA has allocated the comprehension-optional codepoint 0x802E to THIRD-PARTY-AUTHORIZATION and the comprehension-required codepoint 0x001B to ACCESS-TOKEN. The RFC also registers the stun-key well-known URI suffix, with the IETF as change controller.
sections.eli5: The two new labels were given official numbers in the shared list, so every STUN program uses the same ones.
